Common tube-nosed fruit bats, Nyctimene albiventer, exhibit a relatively slow life history typical of small pteropodids. Newborn pups begin life at a modest mass of approximately 5.1 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.1 grams], a value that is typical for a frugivorous bat of this adult body size. During the pre-weaning phase, the dependent suckling juvenile relies entirely on maternal milk, and the period of nutritional dependence lasts until the offspring reaches a wet weight at weaning of about 35.2 grams [Wwx = about 35.2 grams]. This weaning mass represents roughly 78 percent of the ultimate adult mass that the animal will eventually attain, a proportion consistent with the extended lactation period observed in other pteropodid bats where substantial pre-weaning growth is prioritized. The transition from milk to solid food, primarily soft fruits and nectar, marks a critical developmental milestone as the young bat begins to forage independently. Growth trajectories during this phase appear to be largely determined by maternal condition and local fruit availability, though species from this genus generally display consistent neonatal dimensions relative to maternal size. The ability of the mother to sustain lactation over this extended period underscores the energetic demands of reproduction in small, tropical volant mammals.

Reproduction in Nyctimene albiventer is characterized by a low annual output; females typically produce just one pup per litter [N_R_i = one pup per litter] and, under the stable thermal conditions of their tropical roosting environment at 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], they achieve approximately two litters per year [F_R_i = approximately two litters per year]. This modest reproductive rate is consistent with the pattern observed in many small fruit bats, where extended maternal investment in a single offspring is favored over high fecundity. The gestation period, which lasts about 145 days [tg = about 145 days] when measured at a body temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], is relatively prolonged for a bat of this size and likely reflects the metabolic costs associated with maintaining the elevated and stable core temperature necessary for efficient embryonic development. This thermal regime is a key physiological constraint shaping the species' reproductive phenology. After parturition, the altricial neonate remains constantly attached to the mother during early development, a strategy that reduces thermoregulatory costs for the pup while increasing the mother's foraging burden.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at approximately 229 days after birth [tp = approximately 229 days after birth], a timeline that is measured under the species' typical normothermic body temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]. This relatively late onset of puberty, spanning roughly seven and a half months, likely reflects the time required for a juvenile to accumulate sufficient body reserves and skeletal maturity before reproductive activity can commence. Field records indicate that individuals do not typically engage in breeding during their first year of life, instead prioritizing continued somatic growth toward the ultimate wet weight of 45 grams [Wwi = 45 grams]. Achieving this asymptotic body mass is a prerequisite for successful reproduction, as smaller females often produce underweight offspring with lower survival probabilities. The attainment of adult mass is therefore a key life-history bottleneck. Comparative data from other pteropodids of similar size suggest that this pattern of delayed maturity is common among species that rely on patchy, ephemeral fruit resources.

The maximum longevity recorded for Nyctimene albiventer, based on typical values for its taxonomic group and measured at a stable core temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], reaches approximately 21.8 years [am = approximately 21.8 years]. This extended lifespan, exceptional for a mammal weighing only 45 grams at adulthood, situates the species among the longest-lived bats relative to body size, with maximum ages comparable to those recorded for larger pteropodid genera such as Pteropus within the family Pteropodidae. Such an extended survival period is thought to be an evolutionary consequence of low extrinsic mortality rates afforded by roosting in sheltered tree hollows and a relatively predator-free arboreal niche. Maternal provisioning continues for approximately 107 days after birth [tx = approximately 107 days after birth], after which the young bat reaches nutritional independence at weaning and must begin foraging on its own at a temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]. The gap between weaning and the onset of puberty is therefore a long and vulnerable period during which the juvenile must learn to locate and process fruit resources efficiently while avoiding predation. Mortality during this sub-adult phase is likely substantial, though hard to quantify directly.

Basal metabolic rate in this species, measured via oxygen consumption under post-absorptive and resting conditions at 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], has been recorded at 27.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 27.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value is consistent with the reduced metabolic rate typical of pteropodid bats when compared to insectivorous species of similar mass, an adaptation thought to minimize energy expenditure during long periods of daytime roosting. First reproduction in Nyctimene albiventer occurs at approximately 1.5 years after birth [tR = approximately 1.5 years after birth], a delay that reflects the extended period required to reach full adult body size and reproductive competence. The relatively low metabolic overhead may allow this species to persist on a diet of low-quality, seasonally variable fruits without incurring an energy deficit. The maintenance of a body temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C] during these metabolic measurements indicates that the bats were in their euthermic state rather than employing torpor, which some small bats use to conserve energy. Overall, this suite of life-history traits — low reproductive output, extended lifespan, modest metabolic rate, and delayed first reproduction — constitutes a slow-pace strategy finely tuned to the stable, resource-limited environments of the Australasian tropical forests this bat inhabits.
